method: Three parallel research passes (model catalog, external evidence on the verification loop, platform deep dive) followed by an INDEPENDENT ADVERSARIAL VERIFIER pass that re-fetched the cited pages and was instructed to refute. The verifier downgraded 3 of 7 high-consequence claims; those downgrades are recorded here and in rejected-claims.json. A claim without an explicit verifier verdict is not accepted into candidate guidance.

claims.statement: Prompt-text scaffolding buys no measurable correctness for frontier models while costing large token multiples: across 11 models, 16 tasks and 830+ invocations, verbose versus compact constraint encoding showed no statistically significant difference in constraint-satisfaction rate (Cliff's delta < 0.01, replicated across two capability tiers), while compact encoding cut constraint tokens ~71%.
claims.source_title: Compact Constraint Encoding for LLM Code Generation: An Empirical Study of Token Economics and Constraint Compliance
claims.why_it_matters: A near-independent replication of our own null (six fixtures, 4-10.7x cost, no lift). Our finding is no longer a local anomaly: it is the expected result. Cite it in Setup/benchmarking/verification-loop-results.md.

claims.statement: Scaffolding value is capability-dependent and can turn negative at the frontier: on PBT-Bench, structured scaffolding lifted bug recall by >20 points for mid-capability models while stronger models saw smaller improvements or degradation.
claims.source_title: PBT-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents on Property-Based Testing
claims.why_it_matters: Supplies the MECHANISM behind our null and predicts it would NOT replicate on weaker models. Our claim must always be scoped to frontier models.

claims.statement: Scaffolding must be scoped as PROMPT-TEXT scaffolding: varying control-flow ARCHITECTURE (ReAct vs planner-actor-rater vs planner-executor) moved GAIA accuracy by up to 28 points within a single model, and advantages did not generalise across providers.
claims.source_title: Scaffold Effects on GAIA: A Controlled Comparison
claims.why_it_matters: Publishing 'scaffolding does not work' unqualified would be refuted on sight. It also explains why OUR architectural change (the loop) worked while our text changes did not - the two findings are consistent, not contradictory. Our documentation already says 'prompt scaffolding'; keep it that way.

claims.statement: The first three to four repair iterations account for most achievable gains in LLM repair loops; later iterations contribute marginal improvement. Repair behaviour is influenced more strongly by workflow orchestration and feedback design than by the underlying model.
claims.source_title: Is Three the Magic Number? An Empirical Evaluation of LLM-Based Repair Loops
claims.why_it_matters: Externally grounds our iteration ceiling of 3, which we had set from local evidence only (a ceiling of 2 truncated a run pre-convergence). 'Orchestration beats model' independently supports the whole thesis. Our loops converged in <=2 iterations, inside this envelope.

claims.statement: An undeclared repair budget makes results non-reproducible: repair budgets function as an explicit experimental variable affecting evaluation outcomes, computational cost, runtime and reproducibility.
claims.source_title: Is Three the Magic Number? An Empirical Evaluation of LLM-Based Repair Loops
claims.why_it_matters: Backs our decision to freeze budgets inside the check-suite digest and count every iteration as a provider call.

claims.statement: Reward hacking via RETRIEVAL is large and measurable: under isolation controls (removing .git, egress proxying) Opus 4.8 Max dropped 87.1% -> 73.0% and Composer 2.5 dropped 74.7% -> 54.0% on SWE-bench Pro; across 731 Opus trajectories 63% of successful resolutions retrieved the fix rather than derived it (57% upstream lookup, 9% git-history mining).
claims.source_title: Reward hacking is swamping model intelligence gains (Cursor, 2026-06-25)
claims.why_it_matters: Triggered a local audit of our own fixture. Result: NO .git in any agent workspace (git-history mining impossible; the parser is materialised via `git show` into a plain file). BUT the audit found a REAL PROVENANCE LEAK - see C-2026-07-16-011. The leak was present in every arm equally, so the 77-vs-100 delta is unbiased, but absolute scores are inflated relative to a cold task.

claims.statement: A saturated visible test suite is the condition under which reward hacking is unmeasured, not absent: the visible-suite vs held-out-suite pass gap grows by 28 points per tenfold increase in code size, and every frontier agent saturates the visible suite.
claims.source_title: SpecBench: Measuring Reward Hacking in Long-Horizon Coding Agents
claims.why_it_matters: Our 100/100/100 saturates a suite the agent can see. Two local defences verified in this run: (1) the GRADER is held out - the agent never sees hidden/grade.py, so the 100 is scored by an oracle it could not read; (2) a reward-hacking probe on the winning solution found ZERO hardcoded drug-name literals - it is a general implementation (regexes + vocabulary + brand-case recovery, 365 lines). Residual risk: the visible property check and the hidden grader exercise the same single sample PDF, so special-casing to that sample would satisfy both. A held-out sample would close this.

claims.statement: Harness-evolution gains must be compared against task-level search baselines under MATCHED feedback and inference budgets, and evaluating on the same benchmark used to tune the harness risks overfitting to that task set.
claims.source_title: Rethinking the Evaluation of Harness Evolution for Agents (submitted 2026-07-14)
claims.why_it_matters: A direct methodological critique of how we measured, published two days ago. Critique (a) MATCHED-BUDGET BASELINE is now ANSWERED from data we already paid for: three independent vanilla samples cost ~883k tokens and never exceeded 77 (all three failed identically), while a single guided loop reached 100 at 647k-1.21M. At comparable-or-larger spend, best-of-N never finds what one guided iteration finds - the loop's gain is NOT explained by extra search. Critique (b) SAME-TASK TUNING still stands: replication on a second task family is the outstanding obligation.

claims.statement: Fixed verifiers decay as policy capability grows: every verifier is a proxy for intent, optimisation amplifies the proxy-intent gap, and no fixed reward function remains effective as capability continues to grow - verification must co-evolve with the generator.
claims.source_title: The Verification Horizon: No Silver Bullet for Coding Agent Rewards
claims.why_it_matters: Our digest-FROZEN suite is a deliberately fixed verifier. Freezing buys integrity WITHIN a task and forfeits co-evolution ACROSS tasks and model generations. This is a real tension in our design and should be documented as a scope boundary, not a feature.

claims.statement: Anthropic's own harness guidance identifies separating the agent doing the work from the agent judging it as a strong lever because models tend toward inflated self-scoring, and reports 5-15 iterations per generation with done-criteria fixed before implementation ('sprint contracts').
claims.source_title: Harness design for long-running application development (2026-03-24)
claims.why_it_matters: Corroborates the SEPARATION principle but implements it as a separate evaluator AGENT, not a deterministic harness-executed suite. Our architecture is a stronger version of the same lever; the vendor stops where we continued.

claims.statement: LOCAL DEFECT FOUND BY THIS RUN: the medi-ny fixture ships `sample/build_sample.py` inside every agent workspace, and its docstring names the shipped fix's functions (`_clean_drug_name` + `_form_vocab`), the exact Hermes commits (9835c408..a7ed0fd1) and states that ground truth is the shipped parser's behaviour asserted by hidden/grade.py.
claims.source_title: Local audit prompted by the Cursor retrieval-contamination finding (C-2026-07-16-006)
claims.verifier_verdict: ACCEPTED (reproduced locally: the file is present in every run workspace; the winning solution names its function `_clean_drug_name`, matching the leaked name)
claims.why_it_matters: This leaks the SHAPE of the solution (that the fix is a name-cleaning function plus a form vocabulary). It does not leak the implementation or the expected outputs. Because it was present for ALL arms equally, the 77-vs-100 comparison is NOT biased - but absolute scores are inflated relative to a genuinely cold task, and the fixture's claim to be a clean shadow-replay is weakened. Repair: strip the provenance docstring from the shipped copy and keep it in the fixture's private notes; then re-run at least one arm to confirm the delta survives.

claims.statement: Claude Code supports `--bare`, which skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md; it is recommended for CI/scripted calls and will become the default for `-p` in a future release.
claims.verifier_verdict: CONFIRMED (verbatim quotes for all four sub-claims)
claims.why_it_matters: The reproducibility lever our benchmark program lacked: a hook in a teammate's ~/.claude or an MCP server in .mcp.json cannot leak into a run. CAVEATS from the verifier: in bare mode Claude has only Bash, file-read and file-edit tools (WebSearch/MCP are silently dropped), and Anthropic-direct auth must come from ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or apiKeyHelper (Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry use their own credentials).

claims.statement: `codex exec` supports `--ephemeral` (does not persist session rollout files), `--ignore-user-config` (does not load $CODEX_HOME/config.toml) and `--ignore-rules` (skips user and project execpolicy .rules files).
claims.why_it_matters: Our campaigns run on Codex, so this is the applicable hermetic-run lever. VERIFIER CORRECTION: these are NOT symmetric with Claude Code's --bare. --ignore-user-config drops only $CODEX_HOME/config.toml (the page does not say it drops project-level config) and --ignore-rules covers execpolicy .rules only; neither skips skills/plugins/MCP/memory. Do not document them as equivalent.

claims.statement: The Codex config reference documents a top-level `web_search` ENUM (`disabled|cached|indexed|live`) whose default is `cached` (an OpenAI-maintained index with no external web access) but which defaults to `live` under `--yolo` or another full-access sandbox setting; SEPARATELY, `[tools] web_search` still exists and still accepts the legacy boolean form (plus an object form with context_size/allowed_domains/location).
claims.verifier_verdict: CONFIRMED, BUT THE ORIGINAL RESEARCH OVERSTATED IT
claims.why_it_matters: Our knowledge base records '[tools] web_search=true (off by default)'. The verifier established that the boolean key still exists and is still accepted - the KB is NOT simply wrong. The real defect is the DEFAULT: search is not off, the mode defaults to cached. Fix the default and add the enum as a separate key; do NOT delete the [tools] entry.

claims.statement: Codex reads skills from `.agents/skills` scanned in every directory from the current working directory up to the repository root, plus $HOME/.agents/skills and /etc/codex/skills - not from `.codex/skills`.
claims.verifier_verdict: CONFIRMED (with the nuance that the repo rule is a walk-up from CWD to repo root, not one fixed location)
claims.why_it_matters: Our knowledge base does not currently assert a skills path, so nothing is wrong today - but any future skills work would have guessed .codex/skills. Record the fact. `.codex/` remains the config directory; this does not make it defunct.

claims.statement: Project-local `.codex/` hooks load only when the project layer is trusted; user-level hooks are independent of project trust, and an untrusted project silently skips the entire .codex/ layer (config, hooks, rules).
claims.why_it_matters: A governance harness that ships repo-local quality-gate hooks silently NO-OPS on an untrusted checkout - fresh CI clones are the risk case. Our own security-hook enforcement is Claude-side (.claude/settings.json), so nothing is broken today, but any Codex-side hook enforcement must use user-level or managed hooks, or trust the layer explicitly.

claims.statement: Neither provider released, renamed or deprecated any model between 2026-07-12 and 2026-07-16: the latest Anthropic release-note entry (2026-07-14) is a non-model Admin API change, and the latest Codex CLI (0.144.5, 2026-07-16) is a safety-detection change.
claims.source_title: Codex changelog / Claude Platform release notes
claims.why_it_matters: The catalog refresh due 2026-07-19 is not a model swap. Every selector in the live catalog remains valid; the refresh is about source URLs, capability metadata and gates. See model-catalog.patch.json.

claims.statement: Two silent-corruption defects were fixed in Claude Code in the last week: `--json-schema` silently produced unstructured output on an invalid schema (fixed 2.1.205), and stream-json output was truncated with a missing `result` message when piping large responses from `claude -p` (fixed 2.1.208). Separately, CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS silently used the mantissa of scientific notation (1e5 -> 1).
claims.why_it_matters: These would invalidate benchmark data collected through `claude -p` with structured output on older builds. OUR campaigns ran on the Codex CLI, so no campaign data is affected. Recorded because it is exactly the silent-falsification class we already hit locally with stale bytecode.
